summary:
What happens to the machines NASA leaves on the Moon when their missions end? Do they become forgotten, or do they still have stories to tell?

Our project addresses an educational challenge: reducing the barriers that make science difficult for children to understand and may limit their curiosity and future interest in scientific careers.

We created “Surveyor 3: The Mystery of the Little Explorer,” a six-panel science comic that transforms a real NASA mission into an adventure of mystery and discovery.

The story follows Surveyor 3, a spacecraft that landed on the Moon in 1967, studied its surface, and was visited by Apollo 12 astronauts in 1969.

Through illustrations, questions, scientific clues, and historical NASA photographs, we make complex scientific concepts more accessible to children.

Our project combines science, art, storytelling, and cognitive accessibility.

We do not simply want to bring science closer to children. We want to reduce the barriers that may prevent them from understanding it.

Because a mission may end, but its discoveries can continue inspiring future generations.
details:
What did we develop?

We created “Surveyor 3: The Mystery of the Little Explorer,” a six-panel educational science comic accompanied by a seven-slide presentation explaining our project.

Our project transforms the true story of a lunar spacecraft into an educational adventure for children, using mystery, illustrations, and curiosity to make scientific knowledge more accessible.

How does it work?

The story begins with a mystery: astronauts discover an inactive little explorer and strange marks on the lunar surface.

As the story unfolds, readers discover:

  • How Surveyor 3 landed on the Moon in 1967 after bouncing twice.
  • How its camera photographed the lunar surface.
  • How its mechanical scoop dug small trenches to investigate the properties of lunar soil.
  • Why Apollo 12 astronauts visited the spacecraft in 1969 and brought some of its components back to Earth.
  • How the knowledge gained contributed to future space exploration.

The comic combines questions, visual clues, and historical photographs to connect the adventure with real scientific discoveries.

What problem are we trying to solve?

Complex scientific information is not always easy for children to understand. This can create barriers to scientific knowledge and discourage curiosity.

Our solution aims to reduce these barriers through accessible visual storytelling.

What makes our project creative?

We do not portray Surveyor 3 simply as abandoned equipment or space junk. Instead, we present it as a little explorer whose scientific legacy continues.

We turn the marks left by its landing legs and the trenches dug by its scoop into clues that help readers solve a mystery.

By combining scientific research, original NASA photographs, illustrated characters, and emotional storytelling, we connect the history of space exploration with younger generations.

What tools and resources did we use?

We used NASA's historical mission documentation and photographs, digital presentation and graphic design tools, and artificial intelligence tools to assist with illustrations, translation, and visual materials.

The result is a digital comic that can be viewed on different devices and shared through a public link.

No programming or software installation is required.

What impact do we expect?

We aim to encourage questions, help children understand real scientific experiments, and create a stronger connection with science from an early age.

Our project also shows how art and storytelling can support scientific communication without sacrificing accuracy.

We hope to evaluate its educational impact in the future, but we have not yet conducted a study demonstrating learning outcomes.

Our central message is simple: we do not simply want to bring science closer to children. We want to reduce the barriers that may prevent them from understanding it.
